chapter: Early records, Detroit and Prohibition-era nightlife
title: First record dates and why they were just another job
summary: His first record was with pianist J. C. Johnson, followed by Clarence Williams dates; he explains he was never excited by records or fame and always thought he could do better.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Yeah. So -- now, did you then go from Jelly Roll to Benny Carter, the Arcadia, or --
Were you making other records at that time? What was the first record date you remember being on?
The first record date I made was with a piano player named J. C. Johnson, James C. Johnson.
No, not James P. James C.
Yeah, J. C., who wrote "Empty Bed Blues?"

Yeah, I understand he is. Well, he was the first one I made a record with. Yeah. Yeah. Then I -- well, all during this time I was making records here and there. Clarence Williams I made a few with, and other people, you know, who were, you know, small, you know.
Was that -- was that considered at that time, for instance when you were asked to do the first record, was that a very exciting thing, or was that just another job?
Well, it was just another job. I would say -- well, at that time -- how can I put it? As I remember I wasn't too excited, because it was a --
You weren't the leader, for one thing.
So, there was no disc jockey in those days, so you didn't expect the record to bring in more work, I would imagine.

Well, actually, see, it's a funny thing. All during my career, I mean people always ask me questions. It wasn't -- my ambitions weren't along those lines. I wouldn't think -- because in the first place I was home when I was --

you know, with my family, my parents and all that. And I -- and what I was doing wasn't gaited to eating and sleeping. I was doing it because I loved it. And right not, till today, I mean money isn't my prime object, you know. Of course I mean I'd hate to be without money, but what I mean is it wasn't -- and I think people who do that, there's something missing in their -- you know, in their liking for what they do. Now, like you say about the record date, it was just another place to play, you know, and the record came out, you know, and I'd listen to it and say, "Well." And right now, today, if I make a record today, you know, I listen to it, and I say -- and I never made a record that I didn't think if I made it over again I could do it better. Never. And I've never been satisfied with anything I would put on a record. So at that time I wasn't excited about making a record as such, you know. "Ooh, I'm going to make a record. Ooh, I'm going to get famous." That sort of stuff, no. No. No.

I remember working with Fletcher Henderson down at Connie's Inn. This was later on. And of course there were a lot of girls around in those days, you know. So Fletcher Henderson said, "Hey, come here. When are you going to come and get your money?" I said, "Oh, that's right. Day before yesterday was payday." You know.
